Your agent ran all night and wrote 30,000 lines of code. Every check passed. The app was broken. The loop didn't fail — your system did, because nothing in it could stop and ask if you were still solving the right problem. You already did the smart thing and split one agent into a team: a planner, a builder, a reviewer. That's the graph. But connecting agents isn't the same as putting someone in charge. The fix isn't a smarter model — it's a governance layer, an operating system for your agents. And the part you can build today is simple: every decision in your system has exactly one owner.

→ Countable things belong to CODE — budget limits, retry counts, valid JSON, tests passing; never ask a model to check what an IF statement can
→ Ambiguous things belong to the MODEL — why did this fail, the plan or the reviewer; let it diagnose, never let it decide alone
→ The mission belongs to YOU — not an approve button, the one person who owns what "done" actually means
→ That overnight disaster didn't need more intelligence; it needed code to stop the bleeding, a model to say why, and a human holding the goal
→ You already built half an operating system by accident — checkpoints, retries, permissions; the other half you build on purpose
→ A graph connects your agents. An operating system runs them.

ZE1KEgsm_80.description:
Uber just shipped an AI agent that builds your whole grocery cart from a photo of a handwritten list — and the interesting part for builders is how little the LLM actually does.

Their real architecture is a multi-prompt state graph, and most of the boxes are plain deterministic code. The LLM only handles the fuzzy stuff: reading what you meant, judging which product fits. Everything that has to be correct — prices, arithmetic, availability, the cart total — is code the model never touches.

→ The planner LLM doesn't "go shopping" — it emits a structured CartPlan (item, search_terms, item_context, price constraints), then hands it to code
→ "12 eggs" resolves to one carton of twelve via a deterministic quantity step, not free LLM arithmetic
→ A deterministic guardrail can veto a bad output and fall back before it ever reaches your cart
→ The lesson: when an agent is unreliable, the fix usually isn't a bigger model — it's taking responsibility away from the model and moving anything exact into code

The rule to steal: LLM handles meaning, code handles truth.

Comment "CART" and I'll send you the full breakdown.

vFyvzJLcCR8.description:
Only one spacecraft has ever visited Pluto, and it didn't even land, it flew past.

It took NASA's New Horizons probe nine years to reach Pluto after launching in 2006, arriving in July 2015. Before that, the best imagery we had came from the Hubble Space Telescope, low-resolution and unable to resolve any real surface detail. New Horizons changed that entirely, revealing a surface far more geologically complex than anyone expected.

Among the discoveries: Sputnik Planitia, a heart-shaped nitrogen ice glacier roughly a million square miles wide and up to 2.5 miles thick, possible cryovolcanoes, water-ice mountain ranges, canyon systems hundreds of miles long and over two miles deep, and evidence pointing to a subsurface liquid water ocean beneath the icy crust.

Pluto's atmosphere is so thin it barely qualifies as one, and surface temperatures drop to around minus 229 degrees Celsius. Pluto has five known moons, the largest of which, Charon, is over 1,200 kilometres across, more than half Pluto's own diameter and larger than the dwarf planet Ceres. Charon is massive enough that it and Pluto don't orbit each other in the traditional sense, both bodies orbit a shared centre of gravity, or barycenter, that sits outside Pluto's surface. The two are also mutually tidally locked, permanently facing each other.

Pluto's orbit is tilted about 17 degrees relative to the plane the rest of the planets follow, and it's also highly eccentric, between 1979 and 1999, Pluto was actually closer to the Sun than Neptune was. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet, specifically because it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood, the combined mass of other Kuiper Belt objects sharing its zone outweighs Pluto by roughly 14 times.

Pluto was named in 1930 by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl from Oxford, England.

Source: NASA, New Horizons Mission Overview. NASA, Pluto Facts. International Astronomical Union, 2006 Resolution B5.

shadcn, the god of UI on the internet, just dropped new chat interface components. And before building them, he published 15 rules for what makes a great streaming chat experience.
Almost every single one is about scroll behavior.
Here are some of my favorite rules.
Never move the reader against their intent. If someone’s reading, don’t pull them somewhere else. Auto-scroll should never be the default.
If they’re at the live edge, keep the stream in view. If they scroll away, leave them there.
When images load, markdown expands, or code blocks render, none of that should make the reader lose their place.
He turned all of this into a single component called MessageScroller.
It handles anchored threads, streamed replies, restored conversations, prepended history, jump-to-message, scroll controls, and visibility tracking.
All the scroll behavior that almost every AI chat app gets wrong.
Install it with this one command and you're good to go.

Xnj5ta_JxLE.description:
Landing on Mars isn't science fiction anymore, it's something we've done repeatedly with robotic missions since 1976, though no human has made the trip yet.

Scientists believe Mars once closely resembled early Earth. Orbital and rover imagery has revealed ancient river channels, dried lakebeds, and geological evidence consistent with a past ocean covering parts of the northern hemisphere. Over billions of years, Mars lost most of its atmosphere and surface water, leaving behind the dry, iron-oxide-covered world we see today, the source of its distinctive red colour.

Mars is home to Olympus Mons, the largest known volcano in the solar system, standing approximately 21.9 kilometres tall, about two and a half times the height of Mount Everest, with a base roughly the size of Arizona. Nearby lies Valles Marineris, a canyon system stretching over 4,000 kilometres in length and reaching depths of up to 7 kilometres, more than ten times longer and several times deeper than Earth's Grand Canyon.

Average surface temperature sits around minus 63 degrees Celsius, dropping to as low as minus 140 at the poles during winter.

Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, both thought to be captured asteroids. Phobos is gradually spiraling inward due to tidal forces and is expected to either collide with Mars or break apart into a ring system within the next 30 to 50 million years.

One of the most actively studied Martian mysteries involves methane detected by NASA's Curiosity rover, which fluctuates seasonally in ways not yet fully explained. Researchers have not determined whether the source is geological activity or, potentially, biological processes, making it a key focus in the ongoing search for evidence of life.

A Martian day, called a sol, lasts approximately 24 hours and 37 minutes, remarkably close to an Earth day.

Source: NASA, Mars Facts and Exploration. NASA Curiosity Rover, Methane Detection Studies. Wikipedia, Olympus Mons and Valles Marineris.

3yL7rYKYSvY.description:
Welcome to Unknown Worlds, where every episode we take you to a real planet that might just be able to hold life.
TRAPPIST-1 is a red dwarf star system located about 40 light-years from Earth in the constellation Aquarius. The star itself is only slightly larger than Jupiter, and because it's so small and dim, its seven confirmed planets all orbit closer to it than Mercury orbits our Sun, meaning the entire seven-planet system would fit comfortably inside Mercury's orbital path. All seven planets are approximately Earth-sized, and at least three, TRAPPIST-1e, f, and g, sit within the star's habitable zone.
TRAPPIST-1e stands out as one of the most promising candidates discovered so far. It is remarkably close to Earth in mass (about 77%), radius (about 91%), density (about 102%), and surface gravity (about 93%), giving it an Earth Similarity Index of 0.95, among the highest ever recorded for a known exoplanet. Scientists believe it may have a compact atmosphere and liquid water oceans, though this remains under active investigation, recent James Webb Space Telescope observations of the system's innermost planets, TRAPPIST-1b and c, found no detectable atmosphere at all, underscoring how much is still unknown about the outer planets like e.
The TRAPPIST-1 system itself is estimated to be around 7.6 billion years old, roughly 3 billion years older than our own solar system, meaning if life exists there, it would have had significantly more time to evolve than life on Earth has.
NASA's Exoplanet Travel Bureau has released a free downloadable poster imagining the view from the surface of TRAPPIST-1e, showing its six sister planets, some appearing far larger in the sky than our own Moon does from Earth. JWST has already dedicated more than 200 hours of observing time specifically to understanding the habitability of this system.
Source: NASA Exoplanet Exploration, TRAPPIST-1 System Overview. NASA Exoplanet Travel Bureau. James Webb Space Telescope, TRAPPIST-1 Observation Program.

What if you could control AI just by thinking?

That sounds like science fiction, but companies and researchers are already working on technology that could make brain-computer interaction a reality.

An OpenAI researcher recently left to work at Conduit, a San Francisco startup exploring technology that can use brain signals to interact with AI.

The idea is fascinating: a non-invasive neural headband could potentially detect brain activity and translate those signals into text or commands.

Now imagine this in 2030.

You put on a headset, open your AI coding agent, and instead of typing instructions or correcting code manually, you simply think about what needs to change.

The system detects your brain signals, combines them with AI, understands the context of what you’re doing, and helps execute your intent.

It sounds futuristic, but parts of the underlying technology already exist.

With brain implants, researchers have demonstrated impressive results in decoding imagined speech. The bigger challenge is achieving useful accuracy without surgery.

That’s where wearable brain-computer interfaces become interesting.

Instead of putting an implant inside the brain, companies are exploring external sensors that can detect patterns of brain activity.

And here’s the really important part: the system may not need to perfectly decode every thought.

Brain signals can be noisy. But AI can potentially combine those signals with context, such as what’s on your screen, what application you’re using, and what you’re currently doing, to make a better prediction of your intended command.

If this technology eventually becomes reliable and affordable, the keyboard and mouse may no longer be the only ways humans communicate with computers.

Typing could become just one interface among many.

The bigger question isn’t whether this sounds cool.

It’s whether you’d actually want a computer to interpret signals from your brain.

Would you wear a neural headset if it meant controlling AI with your thoughts?

Let us know in the comments.

TjLzAtnA38g.description:
Proxima Centauri b sits 4.2 light-years from Earth, making it the closest known exoplanet to our solar system. And no telescope has ever directly photographed it.
Exoplanet detection almost never works by directly observing the planet itself, most are far too small and too close to their blinding host stars to image directly. Instead, astronomers rely on indirect methods, watching for what a planet's presence does to its star.
The most widely used method is the transit method. If a planet's orbit happens to carry it directly between its star and Earth, it blocks a tiny fraction of that star's light, causing a small, regular, repeating dip in brightness. This is how NASA's Kepler telescope found the majority of the thousands of exoplanets we know today. But a single dip isn't proof, scientists have to rule out other explanations, like stellar activity or a second star, before confirming a planet caused it.
Proxima Centauri b doesn't transit its star as seen from Earth, multiple dedicated searches have confirmed this. So it was found using a different method entirely, radial velocity. A planet's gravity doesn't just hold it in orbit, it also pulls back on its star, causing the star itself to wobble slightly around their shared center of mass. As the star wobbles toward Earth, its light shifts slightly blue. As it wobbles away, the light shifts slightly red. Astronomers measure this shifting to detect a planet they can never actually see.
In Proxima Centauri b's case, that wobble measured just 2 metres per second, roughly walking pace, in a star system 4.2 light-years away. The discovery was confirmed on August 24, 2016, in a peer-reviewed paper published in Nature by a team of 31 scientists led by Guillem Anglada-Escudé.
Scientists didn't need to see this planet to know it exists. They only needed to see its effect.
Source: Anglada-Escudé, G. et al. (2016). Nature, A Terrestrial Planet Candidate in a Temperate Orbit Around Proxima Centauri. NASA Exoplanet Exploration, Detection Methods. ESO, Pale Red Dot Project.

uUIJPWsHD38.description:
AI can process an incredible amount of information, but more context doesn’t always mean better answers.

In fact, one of the interesting problems researchers and engineers are working on is what happens when AI systems are given too much information at once.

When you give models like ChatGPT or Claude huge amounts of PDFs, prompts, instructions, documents, and other context, all of that information can enter the model’s context window, which you can think of as its working memory.

But here’s the problem:

As the context becomes larger, it can become harder for the AI to identify the information that actually matters, connect the relevant pieces together, and reason accurately across everything it has been given.

This is broadly related to what people describe as context degradation.

One famous example is the Lost in the Middle problem.

The basic idea is that important information placed in the middle of a long context can sometimes be used less effectively than information positioned near the beginning or end.

And this becomes a major challenge as AI systems are expected to work with increasingly large amounts of information.

So how do engineers deal with it?

One approach is RAG, or Retrieval-Augmented Generation, where relevant information is retrieved instead of simply stuffing an entire knowledge base into the model’s context.

Another newer and interesting direction is Recursive Language Models, or RLMs, which explore ways of handling large amounts of context through recursive processing rather than treating everything as one giant prompt.

The bigger opportunity is obvious:

As AI agents start working with larger codebases, company knowledge, documentation, databases, and long-running tasks, efficient context management could become one of the most important problems in AI engineering.

And whoever figures out how to reliably give AI access to huge amounts of information without sacrificing reasoning quality could unlock some very powerful applications.

2VgKrwzmfBM.description:
Touching the Sun sounds impossible. It isn't, NASA's Parker Solar Probe has already flown directly through its corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere, becoming the first spacecraft to do so.

The Sun holds 99.8% of the entire solar system's mass. Every planet, moon, comet, asteroid, and particle of dust combined accounts for the remaining 0.2%. By volume, the Sun is large enough to hold approximately 1.3 million Earths.

Surface temperature averages around 5,500°C. At the core, temperatures reach roughly 15 million°C, hot enough to sustain thermonuclear fusion, where hydrogen atoms fuse into helium, releasing the energy that powers the entire solar system. The Sun is approximately 4.5 billion years old and is thought to be roughly halfway through its total lifespan. As it ages and its hydrogen fuel depletes, it will begin fusing helium into carbon, a transition that will cause it to expand into a red giant large enough to exceed Earth's current orbit.

One of the strangest unresolved questions in solar physics is the coronal heating problem. The Sun's visible surface, the photosphere, sits at around 5,500°C. Its outer atmosphere, the corona, reaches temperatures up to 200 times hotter, sometimes exceeding a million degrees. This defies basic thermodynamic intuition, temperature should decrease with distance from a heat source, not increase. First documented in 1939, the mechanism behind this remains actively debated among solar physicists, with leading theories pointing to magnetic wave activity and small-scale explosive events called nanoflares.

Despite its dominance over our solar system, the Sun is far from the largest star known. Stephenson 2-18, a red hypergiant located in the constellation Scutum, is estimated by some studies to have a volume roughly 10 billion times that of the Sun, though its exact size remains genuinely disputed among astronomers, with some analyses questioning whether it's even a confirmed member of the cluster used to estimate its distance.

Source: NASA Solar System Exploration, In Depth: Sun. NASA Parker Solar Probe Mission. Sky at Night Magazine, The Coronal Heating Problem. Simple English Wikipedia, Stephenson 2-18.

For the first time, scientists have demonstrated how AI can be used to design viruses that don't naturally exist, opening up a fascinating and potentially controversial new direction for biology.

The AI model involved is called Evo. Its architecture is inspired by the same general idea behind language models like ChatGPT, but instead of predicting the next word, it works with DNA sequences.

Evo was trained on approximately 9.3 trillion DNA letters from a wide range of biological sources, including bacteria, plants, animals, and microbes.

Researchers then used the model to generate new versions of a bacteriophage, a type of virus that specifically targets bacteria.

The scale of the experiment is what makes the story particularly interesting.

The researchers generated around 700,000 candidate sequences, selected a smaller group for laboratory testing, and found that 60 candidates produced replicating viruses.

Some of the resulting viruses also showed performance characteristics that compared favorably with the natural version.

So why does this matter?

One major problem facing medicine is antibiotic resistance. As bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics, scientists are looking for alternative ways to target harmful bacteria.

That's where phages, or bacteriophages, become interesting. These viruses naturally infect bacteria, making them a potential tool for targeting bacterial infections.

But bacteria can evolve resistance to phages too.

The long-term idea is that AI could potentially help researchers explore and redesign phages much faster than traditional trial-and-error approaches, potentially creating new candidates as bacterial resistance evolves.

That doesn't mean AI has solved antibiotic resistance. There are still major scientific, safety, and regulatory challenges involved.

But the bigger shift is remarkable:

AI is moving beyond generating text and images. It's increasingly being used to design biological sequences and explore possibilities that scientists may not have discovered through traditional methods alone.

And that raises a much bigger question:

If AI can help design new biological systems, how far can this technology eventually go?

🇮🇳 INDIA'S JOB MARKET IS CHANGING — ARE WE READY FOR AI?

AI is not the enemy. Technology is not the enemy. The real danger is failing to adapt while the job market changes around you.

In this detailed Bengali video, I analyse the changing job market of West Bengal and India, the impact of AI and automation, India's unusual economic development, and why the next few years could fundamentally change the way millions of Indians work.

🇮🇳 HOW DID INDIA END UP HERE?

India largely skipped the manufacturing-led development path that transformed China into the world's factory. Instead, India built an enormous services economy around BPO, customer service, call centres, IT services, outsourcing, back-office operations, technical support and telecommunications.

This created millions of jobs and helped build India's urban middle class.

But there was a weakness: many of these jobs involved tasks that could eventually be standardised, automated or performed by increasingly capable software.

And then AI arrived.

🤖 AI AND THE FUTURE OF WORK

Generative AI, automation, chatbots and AI agents are transforming knowledge work.

Customer support, data processing, documentation, basic research, content creation, translation and administrative work are increasingly being automated or assisted by AI.

That doesn't necessarily mean every job disappears.

It means the JOB itself changes.

And people who don't change with it are going to face the biggest pressure.

📉 WHY DOES THE JOB MARKET FEEL SO CRAMPED?

The problem is that AI disruption is happening inside an already crowded labour market.

Millions of people are competing for a limited number of opportunities while companies are simultaneously trying to increase productivity and reduce costs.

The result is intense competition, fewer entry-level opportunities, higher expectations and constant pressure to upskill.

And West Bengal faces an additional challenge.

For a state that has historically struggled to create enough large-scale private-sector employment and manufacturing opportunities, the service and outsourcing economy became particularly important.

So what happens when THAT sector itself starts changing?

💡 TECHNOLOGY IS NOT THE VILLAIN

Every major technological revolution has destroyed some jobs while creating entirely new ones.

The printing press, industrialisation, computers and the internet all transformed the labour market.

AI will probably do the same.

The question isn't:

“HOW DO WE STOP AI?”

The real question is:

“HOW DO WE ADAPT BEFORE THE MARKET FORCES US TO?”

🇮🇳 INDIA'S NEXT BIG CHALLENGE

India missed a significant part of the global manufacturing boom and became a global hub for services and outsourcing.

Now AI is beginning to disrupt that very ecosystem.

Can India create enough new jobs for its enormous workforce?

Can we move towards higher-value technology, manufacturing, research and innovation?

Can West Bengal build a stronger private-sector economy?

And most importantly:

WHAT SHOULD AN ORDINARY INDIAN WORKER DO TO SURVIVE AND PROSPER IN THIS NEW ECONOMY?

If you're working in customer service, BPO, ITES, outsourcing, operations, back-office work or technical support—or you're simply worried about what AI means for your career—this video is for you.

💬 What do you think?

Will AI ultimately create more jobs than it destroys, or are we entering an era where traditional white-collar employment becomes permanently smaller?

Comment below. 👇

A model like this normally needs a server rack and hundreds of gigs of memory. Fareed Khan didn't shrink the model, he changed the way it runs. 3dI1OkJyAMk.description:
If AI can write the code, then what’s left for developers?
That question points to the most important skill shift in software development.

The value is moving from implementation to understanding.

In this episode of Thinking with AI, I talk about the skills that become more valuable as AI gets better at generating code: context, decomposition, encapsulation, validation, systems thinking, and the ability to build changeable software.

When I say context, I do not mean a bigger prompt. I mean understanding the forces around the work:

What can change?
What must remain stable?
What does the customer actually need?
What risks are we trying to reduce?

Those are the skills experienced developers use every day. And as AI handles more implementation detail, those skills become more important, not less.

While many developers worry about AI taking their jobs or feel pressured to adopt "AI-native" tools, simply adding AI to current workflows may not provide the expected productivity gains
. In fact, controlled studies have shown that some developers using AI tools were actually 20% less productive because the time saved in coding was absorbed by bottlenecks in other stages of the software development lifecycle (SDLC)
,
. This video explores how to move beyond "vibe coding" and fragmented processes by redesigning the entire software lifecycle around AI agents
,
.
Key Topics Covered:
The Productivity Paradox: Understanding why faster coding often fails to translate into real improvements when teams are stuck waiting on manual reviews, clarifications, and fragmented tools
,
,
.
Avoid Over and Under-Delegation: Why handing ambiguous problems to AI leads to unread code and slow reviews, while keeping all "intellectual heavy lifting" for humans limits potential gains
,
.
Synthesizing Requirements: Using AI to turn unstructured data—like surveys, emails, and bug reports—into actionable user stories and root cause identifications
.
Spec-Driven Development: Moving from simple prompts to a "harness" of subagents that perform research, pull data via MCP servers, and handle code editing based on precise specifications
,
.
AI in Testing and Deployment: Leveraging models to generate unit test data from user stories and manage infrastructure as code using tools like Ansible and Kubernetes
,
.
Modernizing Legacy Systems: How AI can explain and reverse-engineer old codebases to help teams maintain systems where the original developers are no longer present
,
.
The Future Human Role: Shifting the developer's role from typing lines of code to validating agent outputs and focusing on outcomes like system health, complexity, and maintainability
,
.
By coordinating work across the entire SDLC and focusing on outcomes rather than just lines of code, organizations can remove friction and finally see the 10x productivity improvements promised by AI

👋 If this is your first video: I'm Nick Saraev. I run LeftClick, an AI growth consultancy. We've done work for large brands you're likely familiar with, like Mr. Beast, Anthropic, OpenAI, and a few others.

In plain English: I help people build systems that generate leads, close deals, and scale businesses, mostly using new AI models like Claude. I also make videos about how to do all of that here on YouTube.

It hasn't always been this way. My family immigrated from a Soviet bloc country (People's Republic of Bulgaria) in the 90s. They worked extremely hard, and we were broke for a very long time. I grew up wishing for more security, stability, and freedom over my own life.

I don't have a programming degree, and never took formal education for IT or workflows. I learned it all myself from YouTube videos like you're watching now.

As for my path: I started my first business at 19 in college. We threw events (mostly parties) at campus bars, and charged people for entry. 

That failed to provide me enough money to pay my bills, so at 21, I started another business, a door-to-door marketing agency.

From there, every year, I would start several companies, over 10 in total. I did this in a variety of industries, like e-commerce, photography, videography, SaaS, credit repair, etc. Each grew slightly more profitable, until, at 25, I would start 1SecondCopy, a content writing company. A friend and I eventually scaled that to over $90,000/m. It was my first taste of financial independence, and the reason I'm here today.

Since starting my journey, I've grown a fair bit of capital. To diversify my income, at 30, I began investing in other businesses and advising companies on how to grow in the AI era. These include SaaS businesses, like Clairvo, agencies like Dental Connect, and more. 

Collectively, the businesses that I own outright or are a part of generate over $10 million per year. This returns far more than the 5-10% you would get in the stock market, but also requires a lot of my active time. There's a tradeoff there, but I greatly prefer active investing, where I have control over the entities I'm a part of.

It wasn't easy to get here. But I did in the end! For anyone on their own entrepreneurial journey: I wish you luck, happiness, and perseverance. You can make it!
